# Learning Type 1 Diabetes Through Play

Explore games for ==type 1 diabetes (T1D)== education, self-management and psychosocial learning—and the evidence needed to design better ones. This resource is written for researchers, clinicians, educators and developers.

## Find what you need

1. **[Game catalogue](explorer.html):** compare games by year, language, platform, audience, learning goals, evidence, access and price. Open a row for its gameplay description, developer and sources.
2. **[Evidence map](knowledge/games/evidence-map.qmd):** what studies found about knowledge, coping, behaviour and glycaemic outcomes.
3. **[Learning science](knowledge/design/learning-science.qmd) and [design comparisons](knowledge/comparisons/comparative-analysis.qmd):** how to structure practice, feedback, narrative and progression.
4. **[T1D Physiology and Modelling](knowledge/physiology/index.qmd):** scientific foundations for games that represent glucose or treatment dynamics; not a requirement for every psychosocial game.
5. **[Human factors](knowledge/human-factors/onboarding-and-accessibility.qmd) and [sustainability](knowledge/sustainability/index.qmd):** how to make games easier to enter, use and maintain.

## The central evidence gap

Evaluated games and accessible games are often different products. In a mixed-diabetes audit, **21 of 23 research-origin games were not publicly available**; this was a point-in-time access finding, not proof that previously released games had disappeared ([Reinders et al., 2024](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.diabres.2024.111833)). A later paediatric T1D review found promising short-term results but insufficient evidence of sustained benefit ([Guan et al., 2026](https://doi.org/10.1186/s12887-026-07142-5)).

The catalogue brings product descriptions, access information and study results together. The evidence chapters explain where findings agree, where they differ and what remains untested.

## Why this project exists

This knowledge base grew out of research for [T1D Simulator](https://github.com/krauhe/t1d-simulator). Its purpose extends beyond that game: help people discover, develop, evaluate and maintain useful T1D learning experiences, regardless of who creates them.

Our **sustainability hypothesis** is that a brochure is easier to maintain than a game requiring coordinated software, clinical, pedagogical and design expertise. When funding ends or key contributors leave, a game may lose both operational ownership and undocumented knowledge. The importance of these causes in T1D games has not yet been established.

Open evidence, reusable design knowledge and documented evaluation methods can reduce duplicated work. This knowledge base uses Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 for original content and data, and the MIT License for software. T1D Simulator's source and physiological model use the [GNU General Public License version 3](https://github.com/krauhe/t1d-simulator/blob/main/LICENSE).

A simulation offers a distinctive learning possibility:

> Predict → act → observe → explain → change one condition → try again.

Whether that activity produces durable understanding is an empirical question. The [learning science chapter](knowledge/design/learning-science.qmd) examines the conditions under which practice and feedback support learning; the [methods](methods.qmd) document this resource's search scope and limitations.
